books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which westward expansion changed the lives of Native Americans in the period 1844–1877.

documents.title: O'Sullivan on California
documents.source: John L. O'Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, July 1845. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: O'Sullivan, a Democratic editor, arguing for annexation; his vision of the continent leaves Native peoples out entirely.
documents.text: California will, probably, next fall away from the loose adhesion which, in such a country as Mexico, holds a remote province in a slight equivocal kind of dependence on the metropolis.

documents.title: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Articles 2 and 7
documents.source: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek Treaty), September 17, 1851, Articles 2 and 7, as signed. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The treaty council at Fort Laramie, where about 10,000 Plains Indians met American commissioners to arrange peace and passage for migrants. As signed, Article 7 promised fifty years of annuities; the Senate ratified it with an amendment cutting the term to ten years.
documents.text: The aforesaid nations... do hereby recognize the right of the United States Government to establish roads, military and other posts, within their respective territories... the United States bind themselves to deliver to the said Indian nations the sum of Fifty thousand dollars per annum for fifty years in provisions, merchandize, domestic animals and agricultural implement.

documents.title: California Act for the Government and Protection of Indians, Section 3
documents.source: Act for the Government and Protection of Indians, Chapter 133, Statutes of California, April 22, 1850, Section 3. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A California state law of 1850 that let white settlers obtain Indian children as apprentices; it was repealed in 1863.
documents.text: Any person having or hereafter obtaining a minor Indian, male or female, from the parents or relations of such Indian minor, and wishing to keep it, such person shall go before a Justice of the Peace in his Township... and shall give to such person a certificate, authorizing him or her to have the care, custody, control, and earnings of such minor, until he or she obtain the age of majority.

documents.title: Homestead Act, Section 1
documents.source: Homestead Act, May 20, 1862, Section 1. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An act of Congress offering free western land to settlers, passed during the Civil War.
documents.text: That any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States... shall... be entitled to enter one quarter section or a less quantity of unappropriated public lands...

documents.title: Congressional report on Sand Creek
documents.source: Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War, Report on the Sand Creek Massacre, 1865. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A congressional committee reporting in 1865 on Colonel Chivington's attack on a Cheyenne and Arapaho village at Sand Creek in November 1864.
documents.text: he deliberately planned and executed a foul and dastardly massacre which would have disgraced the veriest savage among those who were the victims of his cruelty. Having full knowledge of their friendly character... he took advantage of their in-apprehension and defenceless condition to gratify the worst passions that ever cursed the heart of man.

documents.title: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Article 1
documents.source: Treaty of Fort Laramie, April 29, 1868, Article 1. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The 1868 treaty with the Sioux, signed after Red Cloud's War, promising an end to war between the United States and the tribes.
documents.text: From this day forward all war between the parties to this agreement shall for ever cease. The government of the United States desires peace, and its honor is hereby pledged to keep it. The Indians desire peace, and they now pledge their honor to maintain it.

documents.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Article XI
documents.source: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 2, 1848, Article XI. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The peace treaty with Mexico, treating Native peoples in the ceded lands as a population the United States would control by force.
documents.text: Considering that a great part of the territories, which, by the present treaty, are to be comprehended for the future within the limits of the United States, is now occupied by savage tribes, who will hereafter be under the exclusive control of the Government of the United States, and whose incursions within the territory of Mexico would be prejudicial in the extreme, it is solemnly agreed that all such incursions shall be forcibly restrained by the Government of the United States whensoever this may be necessary...

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which westward expansion changed the lives of Native Americans in 1844–1877, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the overland migration of the 1840s, the Mexican War, or the federal reservation policy.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about change in Native American lives.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Dakota War of 1862, the Sand Creek Massacre, or the California Indian population decline.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, explaining why change was uneven across tribes and regions, or showing Native resistance and adaptation.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Westward expansion changed Native American lives fundamentally between 1844 and 1877, through land loss, forced labor, and war — though the change was uneven, and Native peoples resisted and adapted rather than simply vanishing.
Context: Before 1844 Native nations held the Plains and the far West; by 1877 the United States claimed the whole continent, and the army and the settler were pressing on every tribal homeland.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 7 show the expansionist frame — O'Sullivan ignoring Native peoples and the Guadalupe Hidalgo treaty promising to restrain them by force. Documents 2–5 show the mechanisms — treaties trading roads for annuities, California's indenture law, homesteads on tribal land, and massacre at Sand Creek. Document 6 shows the promise of peace in 1868, made after war.
Beyond the documents: The Dakota War of 1862 ended with 38 Dakota hanged at Mankato, and the California Indian population fell from about 150,000 in 1848 to under 30,000 by the Civil War.
Sourcing: The treaties were written by the United States and record its promises; the Sand Creek report was written by a congressional committee condemning its own army; the California law was written by the state that profited from it.
Complexity: The change was real but uneven — the 1851 treaty was a negotiation, the 1868 treaty followed a war the Sioux had won, and Native peoples kept their nations alive through both.
